column4: The section explicitly pairs its collective singular وَٱلْمَلَكُ with this verse's وَٱلْمَلَكُ عَلَىٰ أَرْجَائِهَا; here the angels occupy the torn sky's edges and eight bear the Throne, giving the ranked arrival a wider spatial frame.

Earth and mountains are crushed دَكَّةً وَاحِدَةً; this is the closest lexical counterpart to the section's doubled pounding of the earth and begins the same scene that places the angels at heaven's edges.
The Spirit and the angels stand صَفًّا on the Day when speech requires permission; it directly realizes the section's angelic rank as an ordered standing before the Lord.
Humanity is presented to the Lord صَفًّا and is told that it has come as first created; the verse joins the section's straight rank, divine presentation, and root ج ي ء in one judgment scene.
The speakers say وَإِنَّا لَنَحْنُ ٱلصَّافُّونَ, identifying themselves by their act of forming ranks; this supplies an angelic first-person counterpart to the ranks that arrive in the section.

The oath وَٱلصَّافَّاتِ صَفًّا stages beings drawn into a rank with the same root and emphatic cognate form as the section; the verse itself leaves their identity implicit, so the spatial correspondence is firmer than the identification.
After the mountains are scattered, the land is left قَاعًا صَفْصَفًا, a bare level plain; the root-shaped word and the leveled terrain make the ground itself fit the section's straight ranks.

When the Lord manifests to the mountain He makes it دَكًّا and Moses falls unconscious; the verse tightly joins divine self-disclosure to crushing, while marking how an earthly mountain cannot bear that disclosure.

Messengers are sent تَتْرَا, each nation denies its messenger, and the nations are made to follow one another into stories; this is the section's cited “one after another” sense and also explains its earlier peoples as a sequence.
The transformed earth shines, the record is set down, and prophets and witnesses are وَجِيءَ بِـ them; this directly parallels Hell being brought into the judicial scene as something made present.
Every soul وَجَاءَتْ with a driver and a witness; the singular procession shows how the section's vast ordered arrival reaches each individual person.
Hell is بُرِّزَتِ for everyone who sees; this directly states the section's claim that what seemed remote is exposed to sight.
Hell is بُرِّزَتِ for the strayers; the same object in the section is made openly present, now with its audience identified.
God says Hell will be presented to the disbelievers عَرْضًا; the emphatic presentation is a direct nonlexical equivalent of bringing Hell before them.

The rhetorical question asks whether they await only that God come in cloud-shadows and the angels, after which the matter is decided; it is the section's cited expectation becoming an irreversible event.

The verse asks whether they await the angels, the Lord, or one of His signs, then says late belief will not benefit; it makes the section's awaited arrival a boundary after which response is too late.
The sky splits with cloud and the angels are sent down in a great descent; this is the section's cited celestial opening through which the angelic company arrives.
Those who do not expect the meeting demand that angels be sent to them or that they see their Lord; it supplies the defiant request whose answer the section's arrival scene embodies.
The deniers are asked whether they await only the angels or their Lord's command; the repeated waiting formula places angelic arrival at the point when judgment ceases to be postponed.
The earth is exchanged for another earth and all emerge before God, the One, the Overpowering; this directly joins transformed ground to universal appearance before the Lord.
The mountains are removed, the earth appears bare, and all people are gathered without one being omitted; it prepares the exposed ground and complete assembly that the next verse arranges in a rank.
No crookedness or unevenness can be seen in the leveled land; it states the geometric condition that makes the section's “straight line” definition of صَفّ perceptible.

God reinforces the believers with a thousand angels مُرْدِفِينَ, following one another; this worldly angelic arrival gives a concrete counterpart to rank after rank and to the section's succession motif.
At the trumpet blast people come أَفْوَاجًا, in crowds; the same surah later places Spirit and angels in one rank, distinguishing the human waves of arrival from the ordered heavenly line.
Those who fight in God's way صَفًّا are likened to a compact structure; the human battle line makes explicit the cohesion and straightness carried by the section's rank.

The angelic speakers say that each has a known station, مَقَامٌ مَعْلُومٌ; this gives individual placement within the next verse's collective rank and concretizes the source section's definition of maṣaff as a standing-place.

A witness is brought from every community and the Prophet is brought as witness against his people; repeated جِئْنَا بِـ turns representative witnesses into persons made present for judgment, as in the section.
On the day a witness is raised in every community, the Prophet is وَجِئْنَا بِكَ as witness; this repeats the section's “bring, make present” action within testimony.
One cry leaves everyone جَمِيعٌ before God, made present; it condenses the section's successive spectacle into the instantaneous completion of the whole assembly.
Every soul finds its good and evil present, مُّحْضَرًا, and wishes a far distance from the evil; presence opposed to desired distance precisely explains what the section says “bringing” does.
The threatened event is something the deniers see as بَعِيدًا; this supplies the mistaken distance from which the section's brought-near spectacle begins.
God sees the same event as قَرِيبًا; paired with the preceding human estimate, it explains why the apparently remote can suddenly stand present.
When the promised punishment is seen زُلْفَةً, brought close, the disbelievers' faces darken; the verse turns a disputed future threat into immediate sight just as the section does with Hell.
The hearers are told they will surely see Hell; direct sight is the promised outcome of the section's act of bringing the unseen fire forward.
The repeated promise specifies that Hell will be seen عَيْنَ ٱلْيَقِينِ; this gives the section's “before the eyes” claim its strongest epistemic form.
The demonstrative “This is Hell which you were promised” identifies the once-future object as immediately present; the pointing speech is what the section's bringing of Hell makes possible.
“This is Hell which the criminals denied” changes denial into confrontation with a present object; it states the recognition produced by the section's exposed fire.
“This is the Fire which you used to deny” names the object directly to those driven toward it; the demonstrative turns remembered denial into present encounter.

God's enemies are gathered toward the Fire and يُوزَعُونَ, their ranks held together so the later ones catch the earlier ones; this is an ordered human procession toward Hell rather than an undifferentiated crowd.

The deniers and devils are gathered and then made present around Hell kneeling; the verse reverses the section's motion while preserving its core relation—people and Hell are brought into one visible scene.
On that day all are presented and no hidden thing remains hidden; following the crushed earth and positioned angels, the verse states the purpose of the assembled scene.
Across the level plain everyone follows the caller without deviation and voices fall before the Merciful; it gives the straightened ground an equally directed human movement and a stance before God.
When the Lord's promise comes, the barrier is made دَكَّاءَ; the verse joins the root's leveling force to the arrival of a promised event, a compact parallel to the section's sequence.
On the last day the seas are فُجِّرَتْ, burst open; this gives an actual eschatological eruption to the source dictionary's figurative image of numerous calamities suddenly bursting upon people.

In the Flood the earth is burst into springs and its water meets the descending water for a decreed matter; the root's literal mass outpouring explains the force behind the section's “calamities burst upon them” sense.

The day the criminals finally see the angels brings them no glad tidings; it corrects the demand in 25:21 by showing that angelic visibility can mark exclusion rather than proof offered on their terms.

The challenger demands that God and the angels be brought قَبِيلًا, face-to-face, among proposed signs; the section answers that imagined spectacle with a final encounter the challenger does not control.

They ask why an angel was not sent down, but the verse says that sending one would decide the matter and leave no respite; it defines the irreversible boundary implicit in the section's angelic arrival.
The mockers demand, “Bring us the angels,” if the messenger is truthful; this turns the section's solemn arrival into the answer to a taunting request.
The reply says angels descend only with the truth and then people receive no delay; it distinguishes decisive angelic coming from a spectacle supplied on demand.
People are told that they have come to God فُرَادَىٰ, alone, as first created; this preserves individual accountability inside the section's collective ranks and crowds.
Every one of creation comes to the Merciful on resurrection day individually; the solitary arrival sets a boundary on reading “rank after rank” as collective responsibility.
Immediately before Hell is exposed, the Garden is brought near to the God-fearing; the paired movement shows that final disclosure makes reward present as well as punishment.
The Garden is brought near to the God-fearing غَيْرَ بَعِيدٍ, “not far”; its explicit cancellation of distance is the positive counterpart to Hell being brought into view.
In the final upheaval the Garden is brought near; the same act of making a destination present carries promise here rather than the section's threat.
Those who disbelieved are driven to Hell in groups; instead of Hell being brought to humanity, humanity moves toward it, while the grouped procession preserves the section's distributive rhythm.
Those mindful of their Lord are driven to the Garden in groups; this repeats the grouped final procession but reverses its destination and reception.

The disbelievers are exposed to the Fire and told that they exhausted their good things in worldly life; the direction is reversed from the section—people are presented to Hell—yet the confrontation is equally visible.
When the disbelievers are exposed to the Fire they are asked, “Is this not real?”; presenting them to what they denied supplies the reciprocal form of bringing Hell before them.

Pharaoh's people are exposed to the Fire morning and evening, then ordered into the severest punishment when the Hour rises; this distinguishes repeated pre-Hour exposure from the section's once-for-all final presentation.
People issue forth أَشْتَاتًا, as separate groups, to be shown their deeds; this scattered distribution is a human counter-image to the angels' straight ranks, while both serve disclosure.
People become like scattered moths on that day; their disordered movement sharpens the deliberate order of the section's angelic row after row.
Those leaving the graves are likened to scattered locusts; the swarm gives a concrete opposite to the straight angelic ranks while belonging to the same final assembly.

Twelve springs burst from the struck stone and each people knows its drinking-place; the exact eruption root is beneficial and orderly here, reversing the source dictionary's many sudden calamities while retaining plurality and distribution.

God “came upon them” from where they did not reckon and cast terror into their hearts; this use of coming for an unforeseen effective judgment marks a semantic boundary against imagining the section only as ordinary locomotion.

The Fire sees the deniers مِن مَّكَانٍ بَعِيدٍ and they hear its rage; distance remains explicit here, yet the threat is already perceptible, clarifying the distance that the section's bringing finally abolishes.
Heaven splits and becomes frail immediately before the angel occupies its edges; this contributes the opened setting into which the section's ordered angelic presence expands.
The earth is shaken with a violent shaking; it begins another final dismantling of the ground that the section describes through pounding and leveling.
The mountains are pulverized completely; this continues the loss of stable terrain that permits no surviving earthly height beside the section's flattened earth.
The pulverized mountains become scattered dust; the verse completes the physical result of the preceding shaking rather than merely naming another judgment event.
Earth and mountains quake and the mountains become a collapsing heap of sand; this is a material parallel to the section's crushed, leveled ground, though it does not stage the ranks.
The earth is stretched out at the final upheaval; its extension corresponds to the section's prepared level expanse without using the pounding image.

After judgment the angels are seen surrounding the Throne and glorifying their Lord; the encircling placement gives another ordered angelic geometry around divine sovereignty, though it is not called a row.
The overwhelming catastrophe جَاءَتْ; a named final calamity itself “comes,” concretizing the section's broad coming verb and its dictionary image of calamities arriving suddenly.
The deafening blast جَاءَتْ and immediately fractures family bonds; it is another final event whose coming makes an inescapable scene suddenly present.
The heedless person's covering is removed and sight becomes sharp; after each soul arrives with driver and witness, this explains the new capacity to perceive what had been veiled.
Human beings pass طَبَقًا عَن طَبَقٍ, stage after stage; the successive construction is a temporal analogue to the section's spatial “rank after rank.”
Humanity stands before the Lord of the worlds; this supplies the eschatological standing-place implicit in the section's definition of maṣaff, though no linear arrangement is stated.
When the true promise draws near, the disbelievers' eyes stare fixedly and they acknowledge heedlessness; nearness and sight reproduce the section's movement from remote warning to visible reality.
People are violently driven toward the Fire of Hell immediately before it is identified as the fire they denied; this verse contributes the forced motion into the confrontation stated in 52:14.

“Over it are nineteen” places the root ع ش ر in a count attached to Hell; the next verse identifies the counted guardians as angels, creating a concrete meeting of the section's ten-root, angels, and Fire.
The guardians of the Fire are declared to be angels and their number a trial; this completes 74:30's counted scene and shows angelic order attached to Hell rather than only to the Lord's ranks.

A witness is drawn from every community and each people is challenged to produce its proof; this parallels the brought prophets and witnesses in the section's cited judgment scene, though the verb of bringing is different.
Birds above people are صَافَّاتٍ and then fold their wings; the same root pictures an extended ordered posture overhead, but the precise sense is wing-spreading rather than an eschatological rank.

The oath invokes those sent forth عُرْفًا, often understood as being dispatched successively; that succession could echo the section's “one after another,” but the verse does not itself identify the agents or state a row.
Asked about the mountains, the speaker is told to say that his Lord will scatter them completely; this supplies the removal that produces the level, rank-ready plain described in 20:106-107.

Immediately after the promised leveling of the barrier, people surge into one another, the trumpet is blown, and all are gathered together; the verse directly realizes the source dictionary's secondary image of a crowd pressing together and links it to the display of Hell in 18:100.
At the trumpet blast people emerge from their graves and hurry toward their Lord; this contributes the mass arrival that precedes everyone being made present before God in 36:53.
When Gog and Magog are released they rush down from every elevation; this is a concrete many-sided surge immediately before 21:97 announces the nearness of the true promise.
The record is set down, the guilty see its contents, and everyone finds what they did present; the verse gives judicial content to the section's definition of bringing as making something present.

Hell is set blazing in the final sequence, immediately before the Garden is brought near; the pair shows punishment and reward made perceptible together, with this verse supplying the section's object.
The guilty see the Fire, become certain that they will fall into it, and find no escape; visible recognition of the once-future destination directly develops the section's brought-into-view Hell.
The condemned are seen exposed to the Fire, humbled and looking furtively; the verse makes both the presented punishment and the altered act of seeing concrete.
Every person must come to or pass by Hell under a settled decree; following the gathering around it in 19:68, this makes the encounter universal while leaving the precise manner of arrival unstated.
The deniers are asked whether they await only the Hour coming suddenly while they are unaware; the verse repeats both the section's waiting stance and its dictionary image of abrupt calamity.
The verse asks whether they await only the Hour coming suddenly, when its signs have already arrived; it is another direct formulation of expected judgment becoming an abrupt arrival.
After the first trumpet all collapse, and after the second they stand looking; this establishes the restored, seeing assembly into which the prophets and witnesses are brought in 39:69.

Angels descend upon the steadfast telling them not to fear or grieve and giving news of the Garden; this is the reassuring counterpart to the criminal's joyless sight of angels and to the section's judgment arrival.
Angels take the good while saying peace and inviting them into the Garden; the same angelic encounter that closes delay for deniers in 16:33 becomes welcome for the faithful.

God comes at the plotters' building from its foundations so that its roof falls upon them; the effective collapse clarifies that scriptural “coming” can name an unforeseen divine judgment rather than ordinary locomotion.
The Fire is guarded by stern angels who never disobey God and perform every command; this joins angels and Hell in one ordered administration, though it does not describe ranks or an arrival.
On the day all come forth, nothing about them is hidden from God and sovereignty is declared His alone; exposed humanity before the sovereign Lord parallels the section's fully assembled scene.
After each soul arrives with its driver and witness, a companion presents what is ready at hand; this adds an act of producing prepared evidence to the section's sense of making something present.
A witness is raised from every community and the disbelievers are neither permitted to answer nor allowed to seek favor; this supplies another community-by-community judicial assembly of witnesses.
God promises support on the day the witnesses stand; their taking their positions complements the section's cited scene in which witnesses are brought before judgment.
People emerge rapidly from the graves as though racing toward a fixed marker; their directed convergence is a human analogue to a crowd pressing toward one point, without stating a straight rank.
After emerging like scattered locusts, they hurry toward the caller and name it a hard day; this gives the apparently disordered multitude in 54:7 a single direction and destination.

The threatened event comes suddenly, confounds the deniers, cannot be repelled, and grants no respite; it closely matches the source dictionary's sudden onset of calamity, though no crowd or rank appears.

A single trumpet blast initiates the passage in which earth and mountains are crushed and the angels take their positions; the verse contributes the decisive summons that sets the whole ordered scene in motion.
The mountains are blown away among the signs of the appointed day; their removal supplies another specific route from the existing landscape to the section's leveled ground.
The mountains are moved until they become a mirage; within the same surah as the arriving human crowds and standing angelic rank, this verse removes the old topography from their setting.
The mountains are set in motion during the upheaval that later kindles Hell and brings the Garden near; this contributes the destabilized terrain to that presentation scene.
The mountains become like fluffed wool beside the verse's scattered human moths; their loss of solidity complements the section's crushed ground while continuing the same disorderly counter-image.
The mountains become like wool in the passage that contrasts the deniers' distant estimate with God's nearness; physical dissolution is thus part of the event they mistakenly regard as remote.
After giving Moses the Book, God sends messengers in succession after him; this is a repeated formulation of the messenger-by-messenger sequence that the section derives from تَتْرَا.
Jesus is sent following in the earlier prophets' tracks and confirming the Torah; the verse gives an individual link within the section's larger image of successive messengers.
God sends messengers following in the predecessors' footsteps and then sends Jesus after them; the repeated following makes prophetic history another ordered succession rather than isolated arrivals.

Birds are described as صَافَّاتٍ while all creation glorifies God; the root again marks an extended ordered posture, but here it most likely denotes spread wings rather than beings arranged in an eschatological line.
